catalog_quote: List elicitations of quotation forms of underived words and frozen derivations with different numbers of syllables show that Blanga main stress is invariably penultimate: ˈi.fu ‘blow’, ˈsu.a ‘child’, ˈba.kɔ ‘cheek’, ˈɡra.fi ‘evening’, ˈzi.fla ‘exit’, dɔ.ˈve.le ‘tuber’, ma.za.ˈɣa.ni ‘be.young’, fu.fu.ɣɔ.ˈɡa.e ‘morning’. However, diphthong formation (2.1.7.2) and vowel deletion (2.1.6) can generate words with final stress at the surface. [pp. 127-128] ... Blanga has no contrastive segmental length (2.1.1 and 2.2.1), no underlying diphthongs and no underlying codas (2.4.1), meaning that all its syllables are light. [p. 128] ... Underlying Blanga words are stressed on the penultimate syllable. ... When the vowel of the underlyingly stressed syllable becomes V1 of the surface diphthong, words with final stress are generated. Such words do not affect the rhythmic pattern of the language. Surface CVC syllables due to word-final vowel deletion do not attract stress and do not affect the penultimate pattern. Blanga employs syllabic trochees constructed from right to left and main stress is assigned to the head of the rightmost foot. Stress is assigned at an early stage, before any surface phenomena are manifested. [p. 138]

new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress falls on the penultimate syllable of the underlying (pre-diphthongisation, pre-deletion) word: all syllables are light (no length, no underlying diphthongs or codas), feet are disyllabic left-headed syllabic trochees built from the right edge, and End Rule Right makes the rightmost foot the head; odd-syllabled words leave the initial syllable unfooted. Surface-final stress appears only when hiatus resolution fuses the stressed penult with a following vowel into a diphthong.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Trochaic secondary stress on alternate syllables leftward from the penult: in four-syllable words the initial syllable heads a weaker foot (e.g. fa.ka.ˈkra.ŋɔ), and in compounds/full reduplications the first element keeps its own (secondary) stress, e.g. /`ka.la meˈmeha/ 'feather', /`de.ke.ˈde.ke/ 'toe-walking' (secs. 2.6.3.3.1, 2.6.3.3.5, 2.6.3.3.6).
new_statements.exceptions: Surface final stress arises when the vowel of the underlyingly stressed penult becomes V1 of a surface diphthong (/da.ˈta.u/ -> [da.ˈtau] 'chief', /hna.pu.ˈɡa.e/ -> [hna.pu.ˈɡai] 'morning'); word-final vowel deletion creates CVC syllables that do not attract stress; the heavy suffix -lau attracts stress ([a.re.ˈlau]) while light suffixes (-hi, -ti, -ke, -ge) are extrametrical; Pijin/English loans keep their source accent, giving irregular antepenultimate stress (ˈsa.ra.re 'Saturday', ˈle.mɔ.ne 'lemon', ˈpetrɔlɔ 'petrol', p. 144), whereas Cheke Holo and other Oceanic loans conform to the penultimate pattern.
new_statements.domain_note: Phonological word; the deciding statement is based on list-elicited quotation forms of underived words and frozen derivations. Compounds and full reduplications are treated as strings of phonological words with right-hand prominence (e.g. /`va.ka ˈfla.lɔ/ 'airplane'); monosyllabic function words are clitics that join a host. Phonetic correlate is primarily duration (stressed vowels 20-30% longer than non-final unstressed ones, sec. 2.1.4), impressionistic plus acoustic measurement, no perception tests.
new_statements.identity_note: The author calls the language 'Blanga' (endonym); Blablanga is the Ethnologue/Glottolog name for the same language, ISO blp / blab1237, Santa Isabel, Solomon Islands. The thesis is based on 2008-09 fieldwork and describes the language as a whole (the ELAR deposit mentions three dialects; the stress section does not single out a dialect). The eprint and Glottolog date the thesis 2018; the title page says 2017.

sources.note: Ch. 2 sec. 2.6.3 Stress (pp. 126-138): main stress invariably penultimate in underlying forms; syllabic trochees built right-to-left, End Rule Right; surface final stress only when the stressed vowel becomes V1 of a surface diphthong; final-vowel deletion does not move stress; Pijin loans keep source accent (irregular antepenult e.g. ˈle.mɔ.ne); duration is the main phonetic cue (stressed vowels 20-30% longer), no perception tests.
